keyVerseText: Hear us, my lord: thou art a mighty prince among us: in the choice of our sepulchres bury thy dead; none of us shall withhold from thee his sepulchre, but that thou mayest bury thy dead. a mighty: Heb. a prince of God
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun מִבְחָר (mibchâr) derives from the root בָּחַר (bâchar), which fundamentally means to choose, select, or elect. This root conveys the idea of making a deliberate choice or selection, often implying excellence or preference. Thus, מִבְחָר carries the sense of that which is carefully chosen or selected for its superior quality, going beyond a mere option to signify the best or most excellent among alternatives.
usageInScripture: The word מִבְחָר appears twelve times in the Hebrew Bible, consistently conveying the idea of the 'choicest' or 'best' of something, whether referring to sepulchres, troops, or natural elements like cedars and fir trees. Translations vary slightly, including phrases like 'the choice,' 'thy choice,' and 'his chosen,' all emphasizing selection and excellence. This consistent usage highlights the term's role in identifying what is set apart as superior or specially selected within various contexts.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מִבְחָר as 'the choicest' or 'best' enriches our grasp of God's sovereign selection and the value He places on what is chosen. In Scripture, this term underscores the divine prerogative to select the finest, whether in people, places, or things, reflecting God's perfect wisdom and purpose. For the Christian faith, it points to the truth that believers are chosen by God, set apart as His treasured possession, and called to live as the best among creation. This word reminds us of the honor and responsibility inherent in being chosen by God, encouraging faithfulness and gratitude.
keyVerseReflection: In Genesis 23:6, the phrase 'in the choice of our sepulchres bury thy dead' uses מִבְחָר to express the offering of the best burial places to Abraham. This highlights the respect and honor given to him as 'a mighty prince among us.' The use of מִבְחָר here conveys not just any burial site, but the very best, underscoring the esteem in which Abraham was held and the generosity of the community. It teaches us about honoring God's chosen and the significance of being set apart as the choicest.
